utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number, IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam, I see all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, and I think that's about it. From the Prosecution, I see Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer. Anybody else within the column? No. I take it, since the witness, Mr. Joseph, is already in the courtroom and Mr. Thayer is already standing, that there are no preliminaries that you wish to raise. Perfect. Good morning, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had time to rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll make an effort to finish with your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday with your arrival at this OP2 or Observation Point 2. You were there together with your colleague, Mr. Bezruchenko. I believe the last -- the last point of your testimony was that you had been asked to wait. Can you just pick up what happened from there, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to wait in rather determined language, sort of forcibly told, "You will wait here." And then we were summoned, I recall, to go through this perimeter to a back area there, me and Mr. Bezruchenko, and then we were surprised to see General Mladic there, standing there in front of a table, and there were two other members, I recall, of the International Community, a representative of UNHCR and ICRC, plus some other Serb soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I've already shared the caution with you, but if you can, without naming any of the members of any of these NGOs, whether it's the ICRC or the UNHCR, can you please continue your description of what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were summoned there, as I recall, and told then to sit down. And from what I can recall, we had some brief discussion, but the general situation was one of waiting. We were told to sit down there, and then General Mladic sat at the head of the table and we had some -- some kind of lunch was served, and then I recall a Serb soldier was then filming the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall anything in particular that General Mladic told you during this -- during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed some of the preliminaries about how we would conduct evacuations, something like that, and there was some discussion about the actual state of affairs of whether or not the Zepa pocket had fallen. That was the gist of it, but it was clear to me, from my experience there, that of course being filmed, that the purpose of this was not necessarily the -- to get into operational details or nail everything down but for some other purposes, and I recall whispering to the other members around there not to smile during the filming, and General Mladic became suspicious of what I had said to the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did you give the other members that instruction, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I felt that the filming was for propaganda purposes; and I thought it was inappropriate that, in this type of situation, that we should be filmed smiling when we're about to evacuate people and it's a rather serious situation, and didn't feel it would be appropriate to be smiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe General Mladic's demeanour during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sort of jocular and relaxed, and he had -- he recognised me from our earlier meetings at the airport in 1993 and was rather jovial. We had -- occasionally, as I recall it, we might have broken for a moment and he might have asked me some questions about political attitudes of the United States and so forth, but in general it was sort of a positive, friendly demeanour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long did this meeting last, how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to say now exactly, but it was over a period of some hours that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yesterday, I believe you mentioned seeing some loudspeakers. Did you hear those loudspeakers in use during this meeting at any time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The speakers were frequently, if not constantly, in play. They had speakers -- these speakers set up, and as I mentioned, this was at the top of what was a narrow gorge in which the village was below of Zepa, and there was this booming voice that would echo into this cavern, voicing basically what you would call -- the military would call psychological operations, psyops messages, essentially conveying the message that there was no chance for the population and, "You're now in control of an area that's controlled by General Mladic," and I can recall the echoing sound when they would say, "General Ratko Mladic," and there was an echo in there, and it was a psychological, psyops, operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did General Mladic's demeanour change at all during the course of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall towards the -- towards the latter part there, after we'd been there for some time and nothing had transpired, we then heard the onset of cannon fire, outgoing, from nearby us, and munitions firing, and General Mladic and others -- he had gotten up and was talking to some of his guys, but I recall him all of a sudden becoming very serious and then the demeanour from friendly changed to rather dismissive and we were told to get out, "Get out," and this was as this firing had commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you be any more precise about, first of all, the source of this firing and its location?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was coming from near our -- where we were there, positions there. This was outgoing from nearby us, the Serb positions nearby us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was it directed, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't visibly see the direction, but it was rather clear to us that it was -- this was outgoing fire towards the target below of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you characterise the size of the weaponry that was being fired?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had seen -- we couldn't see all the munitions, I have to say. It wasn't that we had -- because they were dispersed around, and as I mentioned, it was heavily forested, but we saw some heavy weaponry but I couldn't tell you precisely the calibre of what was going. But the sounds were quite pronounced and consistent with something more than mortar, but it was -- it was loud volleys, and we were told, "Go away," and we complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe the intensity of this fire that you heard?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was frequent, it was consistent fire, what you would -- it was chronic, it was not -- it was not intermittent, it was chronic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told to leave, and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned -- we had overnighted -- we had either overnighted prior to in Pale, and I think we might have returned to Pale instead of Sarajevo. It's possible that we returned there, initially to Pale, and then ultimately then back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this day-long assignment in Zepa, did you report back to anyone in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported once we returned. We didn't have means at that point -- we did not have communication means, as I recall, during this initial encounter with General Mladic at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you returned, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back to our Civil Affairs and to, as I would recall, General Smith and Colonel Baxter and others there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who in Civil Affairs did you report to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: David Harland, I would have reported to, and John Ryan as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just describe what their positions were, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, David Harland was at Sector Sarajevo, and John Ryan was the acting or, in any event, the senior Civil Affairs officer there for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you stated yesterday that your recollection was that this trip to Zepa, this day you spent in Zepa, occurred on or about the 19th or the 20th. Is there anything I can show you that would help clarify your recollection as to the date, any report or any other document that you think you could be shown that would help you nail down whether it was, in fact, the 19th or, in fact, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. David Harland was quite methodical in reporting, so if he had done reports at that time, those would be a good, useful record to fix the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a document that you were shown in proofing a couple of days ago, and this is a document that we -- it's been disclosed to Defence counsel and noted in the proofing note. We don't have it in e-court. It's not something we intend to offer, but I want to show it to you to see if it refreshes your recollection, with the assistance of Madam Usher. For the record, this is ERN R0123-3421 to 3422, disclosed 30 January 2006. As you can see, it's a memo from David Harland to John Ryan, dated 20 July 1995. The subject is: "Negotiations on Zepa." Do you recall being shown this during our meeting a couple days ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If you would just -- just continue to read, and if we could just slowly scroll it to the bottom of the page. It refers, "Later in the day, Bezruchenko and Joseph met with Mladic, who repeated his conditions for the evacuation of the enclave." And then if we turn to the second page, there's a passage: "Mladic stated that his forces would resume the attack on the pocket at 7.00 p.m. this evening if the Bosnians had not agreed his terms." And then skipping a paragraph: "Just after 7.00 p.m., I received a message from Zepa that the Serbs had resumed a heavy bombardment of the enclave and that the UN team on the spot had been told by the Serbs to return to Sarajevo." My question to you is simple, sir. Having read this memo and seeing the date on it of the 20th of July, the events described herein, are those, as best you can recall, what you had reported to Mr. Harland upon your return on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct, and obviously having been conveyed then, were a lot more fresh and detailed in terms of what we discussed than now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think we're done with this document, Madam Usher, thank you, for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, what subsequently was going on in Sarajevo upon your return with respect to activities or efforts being undertaken regarding the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as this document refers to, the issue of prisoner exchange was active, and as well there was the overall concern with what was actually happening militarily in Zepa and trying to determine the actual state of -- of what was happening there and what would be the fate of Zepa. Would there be a capitulation, would there be a final assault, what would happen? I mean, this was our main preoccupation, along with this prisoner exchange issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, in fact, were there a series of meetings held, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were meetings, yes, exactly. There were these prisoner exchange -- there was a regular commission, more or less, that would discuss these issues at the Sarajevo Airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate how many such meetings there were following your return, just to give the Court an idea of what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was at least one that I can recall where I was present. Whether or not there were more in that interregnum until I returned to Zepa, it's hard for me to say at this point, but this was -- there may have been more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you understood it, what were the primary stated objectives or concerns of each side during at least the meeting you attended or any other meetings that you're aware of at the airport?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what became clear was from the Bosniak or Muslim perspective, it was this "all for all" demand, which included, of course, the missing from Srebrenica. From the Serb perspective, there was this concern that those from Zepa be somehow screened or in Serb custody before being released, and so this became an issue as to what would actually be the status of the men in Zepa. Would they be simply evacuated out, would they be kept as POWs, what would be their -- that was another issue that was of constant concern and discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the course of these discussions, can you be more specific about what some of the obstacles were that may have existed to coming to an agreement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was resistance, there was not agreement on that. There was -- those fundamental points about the missing from Srebrenica and the exact dynamics of the transfer of the men from Zepa. There was no agreement on that, nor -- an additional factor was the exact status of the Zepa pocket itself, whether or not it had fallen or not fallen. This was another sort of open -- open issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you referred to one of those fundamental points being the missing from Srebrenica, and can you elaborate for the Court, what was it about the missing men from Srebrenica that became an obstacle in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been the fact -- the demand of the Bosniak side that they be included and the fact that evidently this was not accepted by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, to your knowledge, was there ever a request or a demand from the Muslim side for an accounting, or a list, or a number of the missing men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, whether or not there was a specific demand, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Included means being included in the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I can't recall, sir, whether or not there was specific about the list. There may well have been. It's just at this point, 12 years later, I can't recall whether that was specific to the meeting that I was in. It would have been logical for them to have demanded that, but if you're asking me now can I recall specifically demand for this list, I can't specifically recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just ask one follow-up question, if I may, on Judge Kwon's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you first mentioned that the topic for an all-for-all prisoner exchange was raised, to your understanding were those prisoners in an all-for-all exchange to include the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This was a fundamental position from the Bosniak side, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the men particularly of military age from Zepa, what do you recall, if anything, was the obstacle to their fate being agreed to during these discussions? What, if anything, became an obstacle with respect to the military-aged men of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the main obstacles was whether or not they would be simply moved from the pocket to Central Bosnia the way the women and children were or whether there would be this -- they would be taken as prisoners of war or somehow screened by the Serb army. This was a key concern, and although I'd be jumping ahead in the chronology here, this was expressed to me later on my next visit to Zepa by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you understood it, what were the concerns of the Muslims were the military-age men or any of the men of Zepa to fall into the hands of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they would -- that they would not emerge either -- that their fate would be considerably worse than if they were simply sent on. Whether or not they felt that they would be killed immediately, I think that was probably on their minds, but I don't recall that being expressed to me at the airport meetings, but they knew their fate would be much better if they were able to be evacuated directly from Zepa with UNPROFOR to Central Bosnia. That was -- that was the main -- and there was very deep concern that there not be this -- any kind of interim screening or holding as POWs. In fact, we have to recall that the whole purpose of this was an all-for-all exchange, and so the idea of them being detained either as POWs or ultimately just being killed, this -- whatever, it was not consistent with the idea of an all-for-all exchange, and the fear was any kind of interim detention, screening, or whatever, these guys would not be exchanged, they would be detained or worse. That was the -- that was their concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, while these airport meetings were going on, what information were you receiving from the Ukrainian Battalion? And when I say "you," I mean yourself or others in your unit in Sarajevo and UNPROFOR. What information were you receiving about the VRS attack on Zepa at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had various military reports about a continued attack on there, a continued attack on the enclave, and there was also reports about firing at and threats to the UNPROFOR soldiers, the Ukrainians themselves as well, and this is what we were trying to follow from Sarajevo there. So we were aware of the continuing military activity against the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether those threats to the UNPROFOR forces were coming from the VRS, from the Muslim army, or from both?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a report of, in fact, both. We had a report that there were threats from the armija, that is, the Bosniak side, that they would suffer the same fate as the rest of the enclave, and which we took to mean as some kind of human shield-type thing. And then this was presented to the Bosniak authorities, who denied it, and there are also other allegations that there was firing, that it was from the Serb side, or counter-allegations, but there were in fact -- we were aware of these dual reports of threats to the UNPROFOR contingent that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you actually ever see any of the individual sit-reps or situation reports that were coming from the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa? Did you ever actually see those individual reports or is your testimony based on what you were hearing from other people coming up through that chain through UNPROFOR to Civil Affairs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, it's hard for me to say. I may well -- I may well have at that point seen some sit-reps. I can't now, at this point, 2007, say specifically I remember seeing them. I may well have seen a sit-rep, I may well have had it simply conveyed to me by somebody in the military chain. Either one would have been perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Thayer. As for the airport meeting, did we hear who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, we didn't, Judge Kwon. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, based on the meeting you attended, and from your understanding of any other meetings that occurred, who was were in attendance?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the general -- the usual negotiators in these meetings, and it was Masovic from the Bosniak side. The Serb representative, Blajevic [sic] or something. I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Something along the lines of Boljevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boljevic, yeah. Because I was not attending -- I was not in general attending these meetings. Masovic's name, I had heard frequently. That was not my area, I was not based in Sarajevo and so I was not regularly attending these prisoner meetings at that time. But those were the -- they had sort of regular negotiators. There was a Croat, when Croats were involved, named Pusic, and those were the three sort of usual prisoner exchange representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Anyone from the military side attending these airport meetings, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there would have been from -- oh, I don't know whether -- from UNPROFOR military or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Either from the UNPROFOR military or from the Serb or Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hard for me to say. The lead negotiators were these gentlemen. It's quite possible that there were not. I'm not sure, I'm not sure at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer,, sorry, before you move on. Mr. Joseph, could you give an indication of what kind of information was available at that time to you regarding the situation in Srebrenica with respect to the Muslim men? What kind of information did you have on the status of them at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, it's a quite interesting question, and the answer is: Rather little, rather little information. And I can remember asking specifically with senior UNPROFOR military about that, and saying, you know, "What's happened to these guys," you know, "Where are they," and the answer I got was that General Mladic had told General Smith that they were -- had been released and were on their way back, were walking back slowly through the woods there towards the -- you know, the Bosniak side. This is what I was told, and I can remember at the time being completely skeptical about that and expressing my skepticism as to why Mladic would release these guys. But we had, in terms of specific information at the time, rather little. And I was asking about it. I was in Sarajevo and I remember asking about it, and we did not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one final question before we move on, sir. Was there a military -- a VRS liaison officer that you recall being based in Sarajevo with whom you or other members of Civil Affairs dealt with primarily?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say "Sarajevo," in Lukavica, across the front line, yes, that would have been -- his rank that we knew him at, as I recall him, and that was Major Indjic, he may have been later promoted, but Major Indjic was liaison officer. And I can't recall whether he would present in those prisoner exchange meetings or not, that detail I can't recall. But we had frequent contact and it was rather normal and civil contact we had with Major Indjic

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he was based in what was known as the Lukavica Barracks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Lukavica Barracks which was across the line there. That was in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, did you return to Zepa? You've already alluded to a second trip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We ultimately then were told that the military situation had changed and that there had been a surrender and that, therefore, we -- UNPROFOR could and would return to effect the evacuation. And so we were summoned a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, were you aware of, number one, where that surrender had been effected or agreed to either as a result of the meetings in Sarajevo or by locals in Zepa? At the time, did you know one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, we had no definitive information about whether or not there had formally been a surrender. There might have been reports at the time of -- that there had been a surrender, but we had nothing definitive about that. We only knew that we were summoned again, we were given the green light again, to go back and make this evacuation. And as I said before, the movement into Republika Srpska was inordinately difficult, only obtained with permission, and even with permission, in great difficulty, so that was -- the actual status of it was almost secondary to the fact that we had the green light to go back and try to get the people out. That was the -- that was our focus and that was our main mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you departed for Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been on or about the 23rd, something like that, but it's hard -- again, it's hard for me, without reference to memoranda, it's hard for me to now recall the specific dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll see how we do, and maybe we'll have to pull one out. Now, do you remember approximately what time of the day you left Sarajevo, and were you alone?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's hard to recall what time of day. I was not alone, it was the same complement. It was me and Mr. Bezruchenko again in our same vehicle. We may have -- it was either the first time or maybe it was this time, we went again via Pale and we stopped in at UNHCR. I made it a point for us to stop in at UNHCR because -- in fact, it probably would have been Pale, because UNHCR had been at the earlier meeting, and then we got information that, in fact, UNHCR would not be participating in the evacuation. And so Viktor and I made it a point to meet with the UNHCR people and try to understand what their reasons were for not going and also to get from them direction as to how to proceed, because ordinarily they would be in the lead on -- on the key aspects of moving displaced persons around, and so we would have to assume that role, and so we needed -- we needed to consult them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Without divulging any individuals' names, please describe for the Trial Chamber what they told you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall is that we were told that there had been a decision made by UNHCR that they would not participate in this because they don't -- they don't want to be accused in assisting in ethnic cleansing. That is what we were told by this officer. And then we said, "Okay, so we are going to have -- we in Civil Affairs, we'll have to assume your role," basically, because we'll be the ones advising and guiding the UNPROFOR military and watching what the Serbs are doing, so, "What should we do?" And the main point we were told is that under international humanitarian law, that you have to -- you have to determine that the person is leaving of their own volition. This is the main point that we were told, that you should -- you should make that determination of their own volition. And so we had that in our minds, and plus I had other concerns of my experience in Tuzla when we had seen the state of mind and emotion of the women who had arrived from Srebrenica and the fact that there had been women missing. So I had accountability in my mind as well from my own experience, but this is what the UNHCR had stressed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this instruction to you from UNHCR that a determination needed to be made that -- let me just make sure I'm getting your words right -- that they were leaving of their own volition, what were the concerns of UNHCR in conveying that specific information to you, that you had to make sure that these individuals were "leaving on their own volition"? Why were they telling you that that needed to be done?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, presumably drawing from their understanding of the law of, of international humanitarian law, that you only move people, you do not deport and forcibly uproot people, that that's contrary; that the movements have to be voluntary, that otherwise it's in contravention to international humanitarian law. That presumably -- we didn't go into great detail as to the legal underpinnings. This was -- we had an operational mindset, and this is what -- how they instructed us what you should do. "You should attempt to make that determination of volition."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that tied to why they did not want to, as you recounted, be part of ethnic cleansing themselves?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. Again, this -- the individual we spoke to was at a lower level. He wasn't the decision-maker on that. But it was clear from what I recall him saying, that -- the individual, that they did not want to be accused of ethnic cleansing and that quite possibly they might have inferred and known that this would not be purely voluntary movement. So it's quite possible, but that's not something that I could have obtained the full reasoning from this individual who is not a decision-maker.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time you reached Zepa that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we had -- we could only leave from Pale, so it still took quite some time to go through Rogatica and down there, although if you look on a map, the distances are not that long these days. In those days, it seemed like an eternity with countless check-points and check-point searches and questioning as to what we were doing, why we were there, what was our nationality, et cetera. So the movements took quite some time, and I don't think we arrived back there, I think, until probably late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you arrive, specifically?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back at that same OP2, Observation Point 2, the same point from where we had met General Mladic the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was it OP2? Why was that your destination?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was as far as we were permitted to go. That was -- that was the staging area. That was the point where -- that was where we were once again told to stop there and to meet and discuss, and again we saw General Mladic there; and it was a different atmosphere, though, I should say, from the last time, where there was one of waiting. This time, there was movement. You could see there was movement up and down before, and I don't think the speakers -- I don't remember, but I don't think the speakers, they weren't doing that anymore. So it was much more of an operational atmosphere in terms of movement than the last time, which was static, and then this volley of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "movement," to are you referring to, movement of what?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicles. There were certain military vehicles that were moving about, up and down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you said you saw General Mladic there. Did you have any discussions with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't recall the full nature of any discussions. I know I can picture him there and then telling us at one point to -- to go down, and obviously we would have discussed with him something about the dynamics of the evacuation, when it would commence, you know, who would do what. We would have had some kind of conversation with him about that, and then we would have proceeded. When he gave us the okay, then we -- we drove down. But I believe it was nightfall by the time we actually entered down the steep road into Zepa, I believe it was nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do once you reached the town centre?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- as I recall, it was dark, completely dark, and we went to the UNPROFOR compound there, which was in the schoolhouse, schoolyard; and that's where we billeted there. This is where the Ukrainian contingent was, and we billeted there. And I can recall, over candlelight and some MREs or some kind of meager dinner that we had with some of the Bosniak leadership there, civilian leadership there. I can recall a conversation with them just in general terms about what the situation was and what the situation had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of any of these Muslim leaders with whom you met?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was Torlak, Hamdija Torlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Torlak hold any position or office that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forget his exact title. I don't recall now his exact position, but he had a position of leadership there, and we were there and had this conversation with him about what was going on and obviously telling him what we were going to do and try to do and prevent, et cetera, this kind of thing, what our approach was. And I can also remember just a wider conversation with him about what their existence had been like in that isolated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall with any specificity anything that Mr. Torlak told you during this dinner over candlelight?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, no, it's hard for me to recall anything more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know why you had to sit there by candlelight, as opposed to electric lights or any other power?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, there wasn't power there; and if UNPROFOR had a generator, if they had one, I don't recall that it was functioning. I just recall that it was dark and we were there and had this sort of eerie thing, because -- not that dark is any surprise in wartime Bosnia, but it was a place where we had never been before; and so we were entering this place where we had never been before at night and not having any even visual awareness of really what it looked like or what the condition was, so that part I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll discuss some of these individuals perhaps a little later, but do you remember meeting, either this evening or later on, a man named -- by the name of Hajric?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I met him that evening. It's possible, but I don't believe I met Hajric, who was both hodza and mayor, as we were introduced to him, and rather young, until later. It might not have been that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To make it clear, by "hodza," you mean a cleric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on the evening of this night when you arrived, did you see any civilians being transported out of the enclave at any time either from the time you arrived to this evening meeting in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a recollection of when we first went down there at night, of some vehicles moving by us. My memory is there were more military vehicles and I may have seen some -- may or may not have seen some civilians on them. I have a memory that there were some vehicles that were leaving at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "military vehicles," are you referring to VRS vehicles or --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- UNPROFOR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: VRS, yes, but I do not recall -- I do not recall any mass movement of, you know, buses, or trucks, or something like that with civilians. I do not recall that at all, and I think I would probably have remembered that. I don't -- and I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, at the time you were in the centre of town that evening, what other international organisations were present in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: None, only UNPROFOR. I should mention UNHCR declined, as did ICRC, whose participation was limited in this evacuation to the part of evacuating the wounded. That was it. And I do not recall them overnighting there at that point. I think we -- UNPROFOR was the only international presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall a French contingent arriving at some point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do -- I don't recall them being there that night. That's my -- my recollection is that we got there before they did and we were there with the Ukrainians and that was it. That's my recollection at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, sir, you testified that your recollection was that this second trip to Zepa occurred perhaps on the 23rd of July. I want to show you another document and see if this refreshes your recollection about the date on which you actually arrived in Zepa that second time. And with Madam Usher's assistance, we'll just throw this up on the ELMO quickly. For the record, it's R0433795 to 3797, and if we could just go to the second page of that document first, the ERN ending in 3796. Again sir, it's: "Subject: Negotiations on Zepa number 6", and it's dated the 25th of July, from David Harland to John Ryan. If we could just scroll up a tad, please. Great, thank you. If you would just read those first three paragraphs. It notes: "Following last night's message from the Ukrainians indicating that the local Bosnian had accepted terms that amounted to a surrender and evacuation of the Zepa pocket, I asked Viktor Bezruchenko and Ed Joseph to travel immediately to Zepa ..." In the second paragraph, there's a reference to Amor Masovic. Is that the Masovic to whom you referred to earlier, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then the third paragraph begins: "At about 11.00 a.m., Viktor Bezruchenko called me from Lukavica, and told me that he had seen the elements of an agreement signed by Rajko Kusic and Torlak Hamdija ..." Do you recall ever actually seeing a copy of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. It's hard for me to recall the exact nature of the document, but I now vaguely recall that we went through -- as I said, we overnighted in Pale and we would have commenced by going via Lukavica Barracks there, and very likely saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Having looked at this memo, do the events in it -- are they consistent with your recollection of the events as they occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And does this date of the 25th of July appear to you to be the correct date of these events?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. All right, thank you, Madam Usher. I think we're done with that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So having spent the night at this school, that brings us, it would be, then, to the next day, the 26th of July. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. What I can recall is we got up there from this -- this school compound, which is on a slight incline, and walked down -- this is again our first exposure to Zepa. We've only been there at night and seen it at night. And then we sort of took in the actual state of the place, which was, you know, rather -- there was buildings pockmarked with shelling, et cetera. And the main -- that wasn't the main thing that would take in -- surprise someone who'd served in Bosnia for that long. The main thing, the image that's most memorable, is seeing already early in the morning this concentration of women in the town centre. There was a small kind of a centre, and women -- we didn't know what we were going to have to do. We thought we were going to have to go around and sort of pull people from their houses, but they had already concentrated themselves, many of them, in this -- in this town centre. So that was the first image that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe their appearance and their demeanour?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they were very quiet. They were sort of huddled with their kids, but generally they were quiet, very, very quiet. You know, the sort of gaunt look of people in isolated places in a war that I'd seen before, so there was nothing of that that was particularly surprising. But it was relatively calm and quiet in that initial encounter there with them, and we sort of introduced ourselves and began our procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe those procedures, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. As I had said, we'd been -- the two main things in my mind, there was one that was this instruction from UNHCR, and the second was of course from my experience in Tuzla with the Srebrenica women and the accountability. So I had accountability and this volition issue in my mind, and we had paper and pen and then went and tried to fastidiously get names of people down. And we also commenced, Viktor and I, this volition query, and basically going person by person, with their kids next to them, "Are you leaving of your own free will, are you leaving of your own volition," this kind of question, and the women would answer,"Yes." And then we would go to the next one, and she would say, "Yes." And then we went to another one, "Yes." And this continued until we got to, I don't know, maybe 15 or 19 down, and then this woman said to us, "No, I'm not leaving of my own free will. I want to stay," she said, "But who will protect me?" And then she began to cry, and then they all began to cry, and we realised that this was a useless task about asking. We were just simply aggravating them and that they were clearly, you know, upset even though they had been calm, their demeanour had been calm, that this was just a fruitless inquiry that's just simply aggravating and adding pain where it didn't need to be, so we stopped asking that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, based on what you saw, what was the impression that you then gathered about whether these women wanted to stay or whether they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression was clear, that they were -- this was their home, but that they were absolutely petrified to stay. And I should add, periodically -- not very often, but periodically you would see a Serb vehicle would drive by, a jeep that had the Serb flag on it, that would drive by, sort of speed by fast, and then go back. Mostly you didn't see that, but occasionally the Serb vehicle would come in and back with a flag. And as soon as they saw that, there would be shrieks of terror, shrieks of terror, when they would see this vehicle with the flag that was there. So it was clear to us that despite this initial calm demeanour that greeted us in the morning, that there was real fear very close to the surface and these people wanted to stay but, look, this was -- they were terrified as to their fate if they would stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During the course of these initial encounters with these women, sir, or later on during the course of that day or the next day, did you learn whether or not the residents of Zepa had, in fact, received any information about the fate of the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it's hard for me to recall, but it's possible that I had some conversations with people about that. It wasn't readily apparent to me that there was a certain fact that they knew, but they were aware of Srebrenica and they were in quite an agitated state, but I don't know that I had a -- you know, I might have met someone who said they were from Srebrenica, but I don't recall a specific conversation where someone conveyed to me, "I was in Srebrenica and this is what I saw and what happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please continue describing the events of that day, the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As best as I can recall, we then commenced with the evacuation as soon as the vehicles came, and this was -- basically, this was sort of the Serb part of operation. They would come down and bring these buses down there. And at some point in the day, the French military arrived, and so we were working with them. And I recall -- I mean, logistically, it was rather difficult, because it's a one-lane dirt road into Zepa down this steep gorge, and it took quite some -- you had to wait until all the vehicles were down and then to turn around before you could send vehicles back up, and so it was a little bit of a logistical operation. It required communication with the top and so forth. And what I can recall is we -- we had these -- these buses come, and we would try, in as orderly a way as possible, to get the women on the bus, trying to keep names, lists of names, and with a certain bus. And when UNPROFOR came, when the French were there, trying to convey -- get them to convey the information back of such-and-such a bus with so many people on board, and that was -- that was generally our task, and it was quite stressful, it was quite an operation, and there was quite a bit of tension. And if I can continue, I might add that then there was a separate operation with respect to the seriously wounded men. There were seriously wounded men, soldiers who had been wounded in the fighting that had preceded and, you know, the shelling, et cetera, and they -- there had been an agreement that these men would be evacuated separately. And there was, I recall, a Serb military doctor along with a French UNPROFOR doctor who did a screening, and the two of them together, these two doctors, would go down and screen to see that these wounded were seriously enough wounded that they required evacuation, because some were deemed to have been too lightly wounded to be evacuated and these others were deemed to be seriously wounded, and so the French, in a separate evacuation, separate from these buses that went, evacuated out this -- these wounded men, and this is the part where there was an ICRC representative who participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience there, was ICRC's participation any greater than assisting with the evacuation of those seriously wounded, along with the French contingent? Did they do anything else, other than assist in the evacuation of the seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that they did. I think that that was -- their role was limited to that. If I may add, the -- when they moved the convoy out with the wounded, this precipitated a near riot in the town because you have to recall some buses had already left and taken some civilians out. Then there was this military movement that was taking the wounded out. And the women who were left, which was even probably the majority, several thousand, thought that this was the last -- it, that this was it, and then proceeded to stream out in -- and block the convoy and were absolutely panic-stricken that this was the last and they were going to be left behind. And this is something I had dealt with in a couple of other places in Bosnia, this absolute mass panic, and they -- it took us quite some time to try to convince them that this was not the case, that they were not going to be left behind, and that we were -- more buses would be coming later, et cetera. But, you know, we have to let them come out because it's one lane and you can't get all the buses in, et cetera. It took quite some time to calm them down, but eventually we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred, sir, to some French vehicles. Do you remember what kind of French contingent vehicles these were that were --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been that Sector Sarajevo vehicles, and they would have had what the French call "VAB," which is an APC, a French acronym for an APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to buses arriving?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buses and -- there were also, I should say, tractor with -- drawing -- with open trailer-type things as well. It wasn't just all buses. It was any type of vehicle that would -- you could put people in, that's what people got put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall who was driving these buses and if anyone accompanied the drivers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, there were -- occasionally a Ukrainian would drive a bus, a Ukrainian UNPROFOR, occasionally a Serb soldier would drive the bus or some other local person who we presumed to be, you know, a local Serb driver, would drive the bus, either military or not, and we did not have enough -- there were not enough UNPROFOR French present to be -- to be just simply escorts on the vehicle, there were not enough, so not every -- as I recall, not every bus was escorted with a French UNPROFOR military. And I don't recall any of the Ukrainians doing that, because these buses would continue on and the Ukrainians had to stay there in Zepa. So it was only the French, and they did not have enough to put one on every bus, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know how these buses and trucks were requisitioned, how they, in fact, were brought to this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a Serb BSA logistics operation, and we're not privy to how they managed to get these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see General Tolimir that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Tolimir the second -- there were, as I recall, two days of this operation, and I saw General Mladic on one day, for sure, and I saw General Tolimir probably on both days, but definitely I recall a conversation with him on the second day, which is when, I should add, that thing with the wounded was probably -- I can't remember if it was the first or second day, but during this time, yes, I saw General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was he doing, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was supervising and aware of -- taking his reconnoitering of what was going on there. There was -- there were other Serb officers involved who were in contact there with the armija commander, who was Avdo Palic. There was contact between Palic and some other Serb officers, and as well Mladic and Tolimir were around and present and actively gauging what was going on and supervising.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to Commander Palic. Can you describe your contact with him and any activities you observed him engaged in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw Colonel Palic not the first day we got there but the next day when we were evacuating the women and children, and his demeanour first, he was cold, he was rather cold to us. He felt that UNPROFOR had let them down, and, you know, anyway, we just explained, "Look, we're trying to effect this as we understand, but our job is to make this happen as safely as we can." So we just -- we at first didn't have a long discussion with him, but then later, probably in the evening, we would talk to him about the situation, about prisoner exchange status, where that stood, and various other matters, and I observed him and sat with him when he had a sort of impromptu lunch meeting with these Serb officers there, that I recall it was in the UNPROFOR compound, and where Palic was there, and they were having the usual discussion about who was responsible for what in the war, and the Serb officers were telling Palic, you know, "Avdo, Avdo, Avdo," you know, and he was explaining back his version. But -- and then separately we would have our own conversation with him about the prisoner exchange situation and sharing what we knew from Sarajevo, our information, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your contacts with him and your observations of him, sir, what were your impressions of Colonel Palic as a commander?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you describe how he conducted himself during the course of these events on the 26th and 27th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was, given the situation where he was alone, you wouldn't even say outnumbered, you would say alone, he was alone, there was no other member of his military there, he was alone and dealing with the entire Serb military apparatus with the highest-level leadership, I was reasonably impressed. He seemed to not be intimidated and he seemed to be focused on -- with us on trying to see that the things were done as safely and properly as possible. He never asked us for any special benefit. He never said, "Hey," you know, "can you get me out of here," or something like that. There was never any conversation like that, and he had a fair amount of dignity. He just stuck around and stayed there alone and, you know, dealt with the situation, even though it was exceedingly to his disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing General Smith actually in town at any time during these transportations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith, I recall seeing up at OP2. We had meetings up at OP2. He came back there, and there was a meeting with General Mladic, but I believe that meeting would have been -- that was held at OP2, not in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that sticks out in your mind occurring on this day, the 26th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- the first day or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The first full day that you were in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first -- not necessarily -- there was some things that occurred the second day, but as far as the first day, I think that's all I can recall at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you remain billeted in the Ukrainian base in the school in the town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So that brings us to the 27th of July, sir. What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should -- the only thing I should mention is that while we were working this operation there, primary focus on that, the French had a vehicle there that permitted us some radio or telephone contact with Sarajevo and with Zagreb, with the UN operations in both places, so we had intermittent reports about what was going on in terms of these prisoner negotiations, but not very complete. It was rather sporadic, our information, but we were -- on the 27th, we continued the operation, as I recall, we continued the operation. And there was -- as I mentioned, there was a review of the wounded, and there was a screening done, and those deemed by the doctors to be seriously wounded were taken away. Those deemed to be not so seriously wounded were then left in the town, and they stayed there, and frequently one of them, who was sort of their spokesperson, he kept -- would repeatedly, repeatedly approach me and Viktor and seeking to be evacuated with these other buses that were going out with the women and children, saying, "Look, we're wounded too." He had his arm in a sling, as I recall, and frequently, even sort of interrupting us as we were trying to get the women out, repeatedly, repeatedly asking us to put him on a bus. And so eventually -- I saw General Tolimir there, and I sat down with General Tolimir in the town, I recall not in the schoolyard, but actually done in the town on some bench, and we sat down and I asked General Tolimir, "Can we put these lightly wounded on the bus and evacuate them with the others?" And I believe this was the last bus, as I recall, this was the last bus that was going out, and General Tolimir told me, "Yes, you can." And so I told this individual, who was quite relieved, and he and the others boarded the bus. There was a French major, I believe that was his rank there, and I was concerned because these were military-aged men, and I told -- warned the French major about this. I said, "You've got to put a French soldier on there and you've got to put a French APC behind this bus," because I -- even though we had the permission, which is what they had asked for, I had my concerns. He understood, and he agreed, and he put a French soldier on the bus, and as I recall they had the APC following the vehicle, too, when it left the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You just stated to us that for the purpose of getting these wounded persons on the bus, you needed to and you actually sought the permission of General Tolimir. For the purpose of having a French soldier or officer on the bus and a French-manned vehicle to follow, did you seek the authorisation of General Tolimir or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, no. No, sir. Shall I explain, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the -- our understanding is this evacuation, at this point, was limited to the women and that the men were the subject of this deal, whatever terms might or might not be agreed to among the parties, so that it was limited to the women. The presence -- the presence of UNPROFOR was always part of any -- we were permitted -- that was an understanding we had. We were permitted there. The French -- the Ukrainians were even driving some of these buses, so there was no need on our part to ask permission to put in an UNPROFOR soldier, when that was already part of the dynamics, and there were also women on the bus as well. So that part was simply part of the ordinary operating agreement, and I didn't feel any need to get any additional permission on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Shall we have the break now, 25 minutes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off with the group of lightly-wounded men and women on the bus. Did you hear what happened to those lightly-wounded men after they left the town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been told -- sometime afterward I was told that they -- the bus had been stopped a few kilometres outside of Zepa by a Serb military check-point or patrol, something, and Serb army officers had boarded the bus -- or Serb military, I don't know rank, officers or enlisted, but I'm told that they were stopped and the men were pulled off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did the transportations end on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They ended sometime in the -- sometime in the mid-afternoon. That was when that last convoy went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just add one thing. You asked what did I know about what happened to the lightly-wounded men, and I said that when the bus -- that I had heard later that the bus was stopped by a Serb army patrol and they were pulled off. I should add that I was told later they went missing, all or most of them went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period from the 25th of July onward, on the occasions when you were at the Ukrainian base at the school in the town centre, can you describe for the Trial Chamber the freedom of movement the Serb soldiers had inside that UN base?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near -- near complete. I can recall frequent movement in and out of the compound. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned one lunch, I believe it was, where there were some VRS officers or soldiers around Colonel Palic. Did you see any high-level VRS officers at the school from the 25th on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall -- I recall General Mladic coming in there at some point; not at that specific lunch. I don't think he was there at that specific lunch, but I recall General Mladic being in there. I can picture General Tolimir in the town area, but he might have wandered in there as well, but I sort of have a specific memory of General Mladic being in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe what you observed General Mladic doing when he was down in the town centre? How would you characterise what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his demeanour was triumphant. He was surveying the success of the operation and was observing what was going on there. He wasn't -- General Tolimir was more involved on sort of operational things, but he was touring around. That's what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, who ultimately was in control of this operation to move out the population?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we always understood General Mladic was the senior authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the ground, as you saw it, who was in charge in town on the days that the population was being moved out?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no -- I don't know that there was any, you know, individual who was present there all the time to be operationally met, it wasn't someone who we had to constantly run. Sometimes Tolimir was there, sometimes he wasn't. There was some other Serb officials who would come and go, but basically the -- I can't really recall our main means, but we were in communication with them and the vehicles came, and we were boarding the women, doing the procedure without, as I can remember, a defined point of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But based on your observations and your contacts with the various VRS officers during this period of time, did it appear to you that any one of them or one among them had been delegated the primary responsibility of overseeing this operation in the town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew, when General Tolimir was there, that he had senior authority. That's why I went to him about the lightly wounded. But I can't say that he was constantly overseeing the operation, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on the 19th of July, going -- or, I'm sorry, on the 20th of July, when you first went to Zepa, and then again when you returned on the 25th onward, can you tell the Trial Chamber who appeared to you to be in control of the UN Observation Post 2?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serb military. It was not the Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the 27th, the last day on which the population was moved out, do you recall seeing Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, the last time you saw Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, we had had frequent contact and conversation with him over that period, especially in the evening, and -- and at times during the operations, and then on the last day I was in the compound there after the last bus had left, the last convoys -- or convoy had left, and we moved back from the town centre back up the incline to the school area, which was the UNPROFOR compound there, and Palic was there inside the compound. And I was on the phone with Zagreb, by our UN -- my contact in Zagreb at the UN headquarters when -- actually, just prior to that Palic had said, "Look, look," and seemingly out of nowhere there was an advance of Serb infantry who were overtaking the town and proceeding up into the hills. He said, "Look, look, look," and we turned around and could see -- this was after -- just after this bus had left. There was an advance of Serb infantry presumably in pursuit of the men who were in the hills. And then, subsequent to that, I got on the phone to report to this official at the UN headquarters in Zagreb; and while I was on the phone, perhaps the distance to that door over there, maybe slightly more, to the gate, two Serb soldiers came who appeared to be more heavily armed than typical, as I recall; and a quite aggressive demeanour, approached and demanded Palic, and Viktor Bezruchenko went to the gate there. There was still this nominal gate there, and spoke to them. And Palic approached, and they took Palic. And I happened to be on the line witnessing this and passed this along realtime to our colleagues up in -- at the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one thing for the record. You pointed to a door in the courtroom. If you could just roughly estimate the distance between yourself and Commander Palic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, going from memory, not more than 30 metres or so, approximately. I'm going from memory, but, I mean, this was visible -- readily visible in front -- in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so what happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- they went away with them, and I asked Viktor what they had said, and he said -- as I recall, Viktor told me they said something about, "Oh, he's going to meet with Palic -- with Mladic." They want Palic to meet with Mladic, so -- and I was -- especially their demeanour and the fact they seized him and the overall context, I was quite concerned, as was Viktor. And shortly thereafter, we got into our vehicle and we gave pursuit. Of course, they had already taken him and had a lead, but we gave pursuit, didn't see their vehicle, but made our way back up through the gorge up to the top to OP2 and to whomever we could find there - Mladic wasn't there - and to make it known that we're asking, you know, "Where's Palic, where is this guy," and we want to know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. These two soldiers that appeared, you described them as more heavily armed than typical, and who demanded Palic, did they have any insignia that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, and I was at a distance that I probably couldn't detect the insignia. But I didn't recall that, and that wasn't where my focus was. What was readily apparent to me, what I remember was an aggressive demeanour, they were determined, and they were going to take him. And this was not this jovial, "Oh, we're just cooperating in an operation here." This was a manifest determination and insistence, and they grabbed him. But, no, sir, I can't tell you about their insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did these two soldiers say anything that you were able to overhear?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was too far away to overhear. Viktor was in conversation, and from what I can recall, what he conveyed was that they said they were taking him to Mladic, some negotiations. That was what I understood was the gist, that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience, sir, did the demeanour, the uniforms, the equipment that these two soldiers had and projected, had you seen that anywhere before? Did you associate that with anyone previously?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- in my view, they were Serb soldiers. That was clear. There wasn't any doubt about that in my mind. We had seen, when we first arrived at OP2, that there had been -- when General Mladic was there, there had been some contingent there, a small contingent there, who also had weapons; not AK-47s, they had other weapons, and their demeanour was more aggressive and they were at OP2. But whether or not they were the same contingent, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With respect to Colonel Palic, what happened next when you were up at OP2?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given no information, as I recall. They -- no one told us anything, but we tried to make it abundantly clear that we, as representatives of the UN, wanted to know what happened. This is a guy who had been negotiating as part of this evacuation, and we tried to let it be known, "Look, we want to know his whereabouts." And as I recall, we were given, at that point, no information about him. And I had -- as I said, I had already reported it, as it was happening, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you do next, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we returned back down to the main UNPROFOR compound there, and I can't really recall. We had -- there were still Serb presence there, and we then -- I don't know, it's possible it was that same day, it's possible it was the day after, we had an encounter at that compound with Colonel Kusic of that Rogatica unit, and who was in quite serious demeanour, and we asked him about what was going on. He wouldn't speak very much to us about that, but I recall a meeting with Kusic there in the compound. And I recall another separate event with some Serb soldiers just milling around, and talking to them as well separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, to your recollection, did Kusic take any part in moving out the civilian population in the centre of Zepa while you were there on the 26th and the 27th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him being part of that. I don't -- that's not my memory, of Kusic being part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So who was the highest-ranking VRS officer that you saw that was actually engaged in the operation to move out the population from Zepa on those two days while you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on this last day, on the 27th, were local leaders still involved in trying to affect a surrender of the enclave or to resolve the fate of the men of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, in terms of the fate of the men, this was Palic's determination and decision. There were conversations, I know, that Hodja/Mayor Hajric was having conversations, and there were still these attempts and some negotiations, discussions, between him and the Serb military, which I believe it was with Mladic at the top at OP2, when I was there and General Smith was there. But it was clear to me that it was Palic who was going to make the real determination about the fate of the men, and it was clear to me as well that was in addition to seeing the -- that we were affecting, as safely as possible, the evacuation of the women, that that was his primary preoccupation and reason why he would stay alone in the town, was to continue to work and ensure that his men would get out safely. That was, to me, his -- the reason he was still present there as opposed to hiding up in the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, one moment, Mr. Thayer, so that we try to clear this up. We're still on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the date. Who, amongst the local leaders, apart from Palic, were still around on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this Hajric, who was there, was still there. I can't be sure -- Torlak may have been there as well. I have a distinct memory of Hajric still being around, and possibly Torlak. That's, sir, to answer to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Mr. Joseph, you just now said - let me find it - Mr. Palic continued to work and ensure that his men would get out safely. Where were his men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His men -- my understanding -- I didn't see them. My understanding was they were hiding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Up in the hills, yes, sir. That was my understanding, and I might have even asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would be together with those men or was he in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, where he actually spent the night, whether he stayed in town or not, I don't know. He may well have been up there, because the -- I don't know whether -- how he perceived himself, but in general terms, if you were a male of military age, you were perceived to be military by the then governing perceptions of things. Whether he actually was up there at night or not, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
