utterances.text: Sir, you referred a few moments ago to being present with General Smith, and I believe, Mr. Hajric for some meeting. Do you recall whether that was on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very bad with recalling specific dates. It may well have been on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe that meeting for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection -- again, I have only some specific memories about it, but to the best of my recollection, it was a meeting between General Smith and General Mladic, and there may well have been this civilian leadership there. It's possible, quite possible, that Hajric was there. And it was a conversation still about the status of the pocket and whether it -- whether there had been a capitulation and whether this -- whether the civilian leadership had surrendered and whether this was valid or not. And I can remember having a conversation with General Smith, a side-bar conversation with him, as to whether or not if, in fact, there were a civilian surrender, whether or not it would be effective, whether it had validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. What I'd like to do is again show you another document, with Madam Usher's assistance. For the record, this is R012-3909 to 3910. This has been previously disclosed to my learned friends on 30 January 2006, and it's been referenced in the various statements and proofing notes. It's titled "Negotiations on Zepa 10", the date is the 27 of July from David Harland to John Ryan. If we could scroll up, please. As you can see, if you just take your time and scan through the first three paragraphs that are there, it refers to talks at Sarajevo Airport resuming at noon that day. And do you see the second paragraph, where it says that: "At approximately 2.00 p.m., Joseph phoned to Zepa and explained that most of the civilian population had been evacuated already." And there's a reference to local leaders meeting with Mladic just outside the pocket. Sir, your recollection that you shared with us a few moments ago about this meeting that may have been on the 27th, where did that meeting that you recall occur?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was again at OP2, up above.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it goes on further to say it was your understanding that the local leaders were going to negotiate a surrender agreement on their own, without reference to Sarajevo. If we turn to the second page, sir, and we'll see if this refreshes your recollection about the date of this meeting, it says: "At about 4.30 p.m., General Smith called from Zepa, where he was meeting with General Mladic, to say two things. First, the Serbs had given the Bosnians a deadline of 6.00 p.m. this evening, after which men who had not surrendered would be attacked. Second, three local Bosnian civilian leaders had been negotiating with the Serbs and had signed or were about to sign a capitulation agreement of their own." Based on reviewing this memorandum, does that appear to you to describe the events that you had testified a few moments ago about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes, it does, hopefully consistent with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, is it? Is it consistent?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, it is consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Maybe I misread, you said "hopefully"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, I meant to say that, that hopefully those others reading the two will see that it is consistent, as it appears to me to be consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this meeting, did you counsel General Smith at all about any topic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had this conversation with him. I had -- because I had had legal training and had been a lawyer, there's a book that I carried with me called "Documents on the Laws of War" which has Geneva Conventions and other documents in there, and checked it for -- to see whether there was something that spoke to this issue, because there was really quite some confusion, and I think General Smith also was somewhat unsure about this. It was rather unnatural that civilians would be surrendering when they're not heads of state and don't command those forces, so -- and we're talking about a surrender of military forces, after all. So the question arose in my mind, and I think others, about their competence to effect a surrender when they're not the commander. And I recall somewhere, I don't know whether it was Geneva or some other document, there was something that spoke to this and indicated that it's military leaders. If you're not the head of the state, in other words, you're commander-in-chief, it's military leaders who effect surrenders, not civilian, and pointed this out to General Smith, who took note of it and, you know, appreciated it, was grateful for me showing him that, and Colonel Baxter was there as well in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that sticks out in your mind about the 27th? And if not, we'll just move on to the next day, the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing at this point about that. I know at some point, it might have been subsequent to that, that Hajric -- and probably it was subsequent to that, I believe it was Hajric and one or two others were taken as well, but it might well have been subsequent to that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Whatever day it was, and if you're unsure about the date, was it the 27th -- would it have been the 27th or 28th or sometime after the 28th? Can you be certain as to at least whether it was the 27th, 28th, or a subsequent day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain whether -- it's unlikely that it was the 27th because it would have been unlikely that it would have happened in front of General Smith. I don't think that would have -- I don't think they would have done that, but -- and I don't think they did, but -- so it's based on the fact that we know that this meeting took place on the 27th, I believe it could have been the 28th. Could it have been the 29th? Equally possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the 28th. Do you recall following up with anyone or having any conversations with anyone concerning the fate of Colonel Palic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That morning, the first thing I can remember doing that morning, we had had radio contact from -- because this was the Ukrainian means, these were, as I recall, Ukrainian means, their own radio means, between their compound in the town and OP2, and so they had -- there was an UNPROFOR radio, and I -- which the Serbs were on, so I believe it to still be the UNPROFOR means at the other end, and I attempted and I managed to raise General Mladic by these radio means the next morning to again follow up the issue of Colonel Palic and to ask and say, "Where is he, where is Colonel Palic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what response did you get?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this -- again, over a crackly radio, what I thought I understood him to say is something that he got away and was killed, but it's possible, because of the scratchiness and I knew at the time that I wasn't sure, possibly, because the words were similar for escape -- to kill, "poginuti", and to escape, "pobjeci", they are similar, and especially on a scratchy means, I wasn't sure. And later that day, we, Viktor and I -- I told this to Viktor, and the two of us went to see Mladic's interpreter to try to see if she was present and could confirm this. And I confirmed with her that she recalled that we had had this conversation, and I attempted to get her to confirm which -- what was the meaning. And as I recall, that she had said that he was -- confirmed that he had said that he was killed. That was my recollection of it, but the possibility exists that there was miscommunication on this. I will say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at this point or previously, did you report to anyone in your chain of command at the time -- you testified you had a realtime call with Zagreb when the abduction or he was taken away occurred. Did you report to anyone else either about Abdic [sic] being taken from the UNPROFOR base or the conversation that you had with General Mladic or the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, indeed. I reported this to our people in Sarajevo, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the name "Abdic" in line 25, shouldn't it be "Palic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Abdic" is from another drama that I was in, different era, different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did you -- you've referred to seeing Mr. Hajric also being taken. Can you describe what you saw to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- yes. It's hard for me to recollect the date or the exact circumstances, but I recall a subsequent meeting at OP2 where Hajric was there and at least one other, plus one lone male, middle-aged male, Bosniak, as he identified himself, who had somehow been separated from the rest of the folks in Zepa, be they military or civilian, and who had insisted to us that he was over military age. That was what he kept saying, and again requesting to be evacuated. And I believe the evacuation had -- this was after they had finished. And I recall Hajric, possibly one other individual and this gentleman, and we were there meeting with VRS officials. I can't be sure if it was Tolimir or others. And they were taken, that was it, they were taken, and that's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall any further details about anything that was said or any indications given about where they were being taken to or for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although there was no -- nothing -- we were not told anything benign. We were not told, "Oh, they're just being taken to a meeting and then --" we weren't told anything benign, I don't believe. They were taken, and that's as far as I can say. And when we left, when we ultimately left Zepa, we reported that to ICRC to let them know about that, and the others, the lightly wounded, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In fact, can you recall the date that you left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I cannot recall without reference to some document. I can't, on my own, recall the exact date. I know we were not permitted to leave right away. We were -- we -- once we had gotten word from Sarajevo that the prisoner exchange was not going to happen, ultimately when we received that word and were then -- and were told to come back and try to leave, we were not permitted to leave. The Serb military would not give us permission to leave, so we were stuck there an additional period. I'm not sure how long that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you stuck up at the OP2 or down in town at the Ukrainian base in the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been both. I have a memory of Viktor and I being stuck at OP2, and I also know we had dead time down in the town once -- after Palic had been taken and these negotiations were then -- there was, no more interlocutor for us on their side there, and it's possible we were in both locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the time that you left Zepa, to your knowledge, other than the men of Zepa who you had heard were up in the hills, were there any Muslims left in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to briefly show you some video footage. We're just going to play a few seconds from a couple of clips. I've advised my friends of the times. May we first play P02489? That's ERN V000-1355. I think we're going to begin at 11.29.82. Do you have an image on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 12.31.01. Do you recognise anyone in this video still?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise all four of the individuals and can name three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Please do, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facing us to the left is Torlak. To his left, our right, another Bosniak leader who I recognise and met with, but whose name I can't recall. And with their backs to us, to his left there on the right would be General Mladic, and I believe, although I'm recognising him from the back, but I believe to his left there is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And having viewed this clip, sir, can you identify what this location is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be OP2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're going to fast-forward to save a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 15.20.06. Can you recognise anyone in this clip, in this still?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that that's General Tolimir there to the left of General Mladic. The other three, I'm not sure. It's possible that that's Kusic at the end, but I'm not sure, with the mustache at the end; but I can't be 100 per cent sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now, sir, is play a short excerpt from another clip. This is P02491, ERN V000-3142. We will begin at 45.29.68.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 45.30.04. Do you recognise anybody in this still?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individual, the male in uniform in the center is Avdo Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing the clip for a few seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Having seen the portion of the clip prior to your identification of Colonel Palic and the few seconds afterwards, can you identify that location, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the center of Zepa. That would have been on or near our staging area for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we did not get the exact location of that still. If we could go back to it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the still of Colonel Palic or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, that we have. The still where there's this group of people standing by the bus, and you asked the witness where that would be. I just wanted to -- yes, that's it. It's at 45.36.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're going to begin playing a clip at 45.56.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 46.14. Do you recognise anyone in this still?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- the male in the light blue jacket there is the Mayor Hodza Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any information concerning the fate of Mr. Hajric, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although I understand he was missing. That's-- he was on the list of missing, and that's as far as I know unaccounted for, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you ever met any of his relatives, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I met -- THE REPORTER: I'm sorry, Your Honour, can I just have a moment? My electrical plug just came out, and I need to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. In the meantime, what happened to Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's working out of the office this morning for the remainder of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can proceed, and for the record I asked Mr. Ostojic to account for Mr. Meek's absence from the courtroom, and we were informed that Mr. Meek has left to seek with some work in the office -- in his office. So, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just repeat my last question before we had the technical difficulty. Do you have any information concerning the fate of Mr. Hajric?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I understand he was on the list of missing from Zepa and has not been accounted for. That's my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you ever met with any of Mr. Hajric's relatives?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, I believe it was in 1997, I met his -- his father, who asked about him and -- you know, to try to get energy about -- and information about what had happened to him. That was in Sarajevo. That was, I believe, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did he say to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was quite upset and feared the worst, and just wanted him not forgotten and wanted information about him. That was -- and that the International Community become engaged to get information about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time. I see you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm motioning if the -- with the permission of the Court, just the image of General Mladic sparked one memory that I think could be of information or could be of interest to the Court, if I'm permitted to say that, even though it's not in reply to a direct question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seeing the image of General Mladic, I remember having a conversation with him at at least one point during these events about the -- at least one, possibly more, about the fate of the men and about what would happen to the men and how we would effect some transfer, if in fact there were an agreement made in Sarajevo, how we would actually effect this transfer, because that was quite some concern to me, to see how this thing was actually going to get pulled off safely. And I recall that General Mladic said to me -- I said to him, "Are you -- are you going to let these guys go? They'll just come down from the hills --" pardon me. "They'll just come down from the hills, and UNPROFOR will be here, and you're just going to let them go?" And I recall he said to me, "Yes, I'll let them go, except for the war criminals." And I said, "What, in other words, you'll screen?" And he said, "Yes, yes, we will not let the war criminals leave." And that was -- I have a distinct memory of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And of what significance to you were those comments or that statement of General Mladic? Did that mean anything to you? Did you come away with any particular feeling or impression after he told you that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took that to mean that this was going to be highly problematic and that these guys would be imperilled and that this would -- it would mean that they would have access to them, and I took it to mean most of them would be seized. That was my impression. I did not see this -- that was my impression. I didn't see this as any terms of some very selective thing. I thought that it -- I took it to mean this entire operation would be in jeopardy, and their security would be in jeopardy, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Let's have a revised estimate of cross-examinations. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are where you stood before. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 45 minutes, Mr. President, to an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic, you had not indicated any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, we will not cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We will have no cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll stick to the 75 minutes I previously estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes, no cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you come to any agreement as to who will go first? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, we, this part of the Court represent General Gvero, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. You used the word, twice, I think, in your final answer there, "impression." Would you say the evidence you have just given is impressionistic rather than a factual recollection of events, particularly bearing in mind the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, are you asking -- just to clarify so I can answer your question in the best possible way, are you asking me to characterise my entire testimony or just this last conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your entire testimony is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I would not characterise my entire testimony as impressionistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's beyond dispute that you are recalling events that took place over 12 years ago. You haven't used a note. Is that deliberate, or have you been instructed not to use a note, or did you not make any notes? Help us in that regard, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made no -- as best I can remember, I didn't keep a journal at the time, and I'm relying on my memory and from the proofing that I've done and these UN memoranda.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right to say that there are several other memoranda written primarily by Mr. Harland. They make reference, in part, to things that you told him, but they are, by no means, detailed documents so far as what you told him is concerned. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not detailed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They don't detail -- they don't --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- the documents stand on their own, and I don't -- in some respects, one might consider them detailed, and in other, you might not. It would depend on the reader. I would say they are accurate. They are accurate, contemporaneous recollections of communication that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zepa for the first time, did you regard yourself as an objective player in the events that you were about to become involved in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Completely?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you, presumably, had picked up certain preconceptions and, dare I say it, baggage over the three years that you had previously spent in Bosnia, or is that an unfair comment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you would call baggage, I would call experience, and I'm happy to discuss and provide more detail, as much as you wish. But in terms of the dynamics, in terms of modus operandi, I would call it experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, for example, did you think, yourself, "Well, here we go again, I've experienced events like this in," for example, "Bihac"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of evacuations, I wouldn't have drawn Bihac. I had done evacuations and been part of evacuations of Syrian students from Sarajevo in 1992 and Croats from Krajina, in a Serb part of Croatia, in 1993. So that was -- this mission was about an evacuation, and so that was my most relevant comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And 12 years later, do you still regard yourself as an objective observer of the events that you have described for the last few hours?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- yes, I would -- this is how I would put it: I am objective as I can be with respect to these events, and I would say as well that I'm a human being. We have emotions and feelings as well. And I would say in addition that I have had the rare -- possibly unique, but the rare ability, as I mentioned at the outset when I was asked about my background, to have worked in every single facet of a conflict of the former Yugoslavia, except for the Slovenian-Serb conflict, which was only ten days, but every single conflict, so I would see similarities and differences from the Croat-Serb theatre, the internal conflict between Muslims in Bihac, and the Croat-Bosniak fighting in Mostar, and I drew tremendous experience. And through this, though, whatever my feelings and impressions and experience, I think I was, and am able, to have analytical detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turning specifically to your role in Zepa, you have just told us that your primary role was to organise an evacuation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what, if anything, had Mr. Harland, who as I understand it was your boss, told you to achieve in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: David was, in fact, not our boss. We were -- David was at the sector level, as I recall then, in Sarajevo, so he had sector-area responsibilities, as I recall. And the direct boss was John Ryan, who was at the head. We were -- I was not part of -- under David's team there, although David was doing the main reporting on the issue, especially because the Sector Sarajevo Detachment of the French was involved as well, and David was a primary person to do reporting there. So that's internal chain of command. I'm not sure if I've answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The real question, in fact, was: What, if anything, had you been told by your superiors to achieve?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, we were told to -- there were very few instructions, specific ones, that I can recall at this point. What we understood our role was to establish ourselves there. In fact, one of the reasons we were sent, Viktor and I, was because of our experience, and I think the presumption was we knew what we would have to do; establish our liaison, first of all, with the Serb military, do likewise with the armija and civilian representatives, establish and liaise with the UNPROFOR military assets that were there and that would come, likewise with any other international organisations. I don't recall specific instructions other than there would be this evacuation and we were meant to coordinate it. There may have been something specific, but nothing that I can recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it a coincidence that Viktor was a Ukrainian and presumably could communicate easily with the Ukrainian troops that were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that was deliberate or not. In any event, it was useful to have him there in that capacity, I think. But whether he was specifically sent, it's quite possible that that might have figured in the reasoning. But Viktor, like myself, had been there since 1992 and had tremendous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent were you aware of the specific problems that had been occurring over quite a long period of time in the enclave? And by that, I mean that it was not properly, and arguably at all, demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what extent were we aware it was not demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there was fighting, and, yes, we knew that the armija had weapons. We were aware of that because at one point we even proposed demilitarisation, so, yes, I think that that was clear to us, that the armija had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that there had been ongoing attacks from within the enclave to outside Serb targets; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What do you mean by "ongoing attacks," do you mean prior to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean prior.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that, I don't know. That, I can't speak to that, that part of the history, I can't speak to. You have to understand, my involvement, and in fact much of the UNPROFOR involvement began after the events in Srebrenica just prior, the 11th of July, et cetera, so this is when Zepa became of -- a focus. So what had transpired prior to that, I can't really provide much -- shed much light on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me put it slightly differently, and I hope I can be excused for using a slight shorthand. Were you aware, in the first six to seven months of 1995, of why Srebrenica was such a sore to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica, yes, because -- but not Zepa. Srebrenica, yes, because I was first deployed back -- I had been in Sarajevo in 1992, then to Knin, and then moved back to Sarajevo and Kiseljak back in the spring of 1993, right after General Morillon's famous visit, et cetera, when it first became -- when the safe area resolutions, et cetera, became first involved, and I was aware of sort of the issue of demilitarisation, yes, sir, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you had no similar knowledge in relation to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, sir, I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too long on this, but in terms of briefings to learn about the area that you were about to become involved in, what were the United Nations able to offer you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I think we had sit-reps and had some briefings, but, you know, we had very little presence there, other than this Ukrainian contingent that was there. We had no Civil Affairs presence there, although, as I recall, we had requested for the Serbs to let us have Civil Affairs presence throughout these areas and had only managed -- I think there had been agreement in Gorazde, there had been intermittent Civil Affairs presence in Gorazde. So I think we had relatively limited briefing about the actual situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you have been at pains to point out that as far as you could judge, OP2 had been taken over by the Serbs; that's right, isn't it? That's your evidence, anyway?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I've been at pains, but it was my clear impression. That was our clear impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival at or in the enclave, were you aware of difficulties that the Ukrainian Battalion had faced at the hands of the Bosniak soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I mentioned in my testimony, we had reports that they had had threats and possibly even been shot at from the Bosniak side, as I make clear in my testimony. This was denied by the Bosniak side, but, to answer your question, the answer is, yes, and I so testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest that it really goes rather further than that. Could we bring up on the screen 6D132, please. I'm going to ask you to categorise -- characterise this document. I'm not sure if one would call it a sit-rep. It's clearly says, "UNPROFOR" at the top. It's dated the 17th of July, it's from Ukrainian Battalion 1/Sarajevo to another Sarajevo group. Would you call this a sit-rep?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're using sync-rep, but I take that to mean the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the body of it, please. We see it's at 2100 hours of that day. It says: "According to the information received from Brit-Bat through VSAT phone call in the night from 15 to 16 of July 1995, the Bosnians took us hostage, UKRCOY, Lieutenant-Colonel Batalin, and demanded to give them up all weapons, equipment and ammunition, otherwise threatening to kill UKRCOY company. In an hour when negotiations failed, 60 men from special forces and 100 from regular troops penetrated to UKRCOY enclose and confiscated all weapons, military equipment, vehicles, ammo and medicine. BiH side supported their actions with fire at UKRCOY compound. Only four vehicles left." It then describes what those vehicles are. " Due to the low quality of water and absence of food broke out dysentry. Three men are sick. BiH side threatened displacing Ukrainians as a human shield against BSA attack on their positions." And if we turn to the next page, please, it says, "The List of Captured Vehicles." I'm not going to read it out, but it speaks for itself. And if we turn two pages on, it says, "The List of Captured Weapons" and is very specific as to exactly what was captured. Did you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't recall this specific sit-rep. I recall that there had been, as I said -- testified earlier, that there had been this allegation that they had been threatened and had possibly been attacked. But, no, the answer is, no, I don't recall this specific sit-rep and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you arrived there on the 20th of July, you didn't, in fact, have any dealings with Ukrainian soldiers on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you're referring to the first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first time, deliberately.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, yeah, there were probably Ukrainian soldiers at that OP2 compound, but they were not terribly relevant to our purpose. We might have said hello to them, so the answer is we might have well had some contact with them, but we didn't -- and they didn't seek us out especially, and obviously Viktor was there as a former Ukrainian military and could speak to them in Ukrainian and assess their situation, but that was neither Viktor's preoccupation nor, seemingly, their preoccupation, nor mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this didn't get back to you -- let me ask you another question first. You had not been briefed to ask them, the Ukrainian troops, about what's contained within this rather startling report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't the focus, but I think that it may well have been -- this issue, we were certainly aware of, and as I said, I had a former Ukrainian colonel who had served there with me who can easily detect far better than I -- can communicate with his former comrades and assess their determination. But I can tell you, I recall no sense of desperation on their part upon seeing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that was really my second question. I'll come to that in a moment. My first question is: This is presumably a genuine report. This genuine report, presumably, had got through to the people who had sent you on this mission. Am I right to find it remarkable that the information contained within this report hadn't gone to you, the man who was about to go into the enclave, so that you knew exactly what was going on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're quite right to focus on this, and I think it's entirely fair to ask this. To put it into context, let's remember my title, "Civil Affairs Officer," so I'm not there to specifically look after the needs of the military side. It wasn't my role, nor Viktor's, although he happened to be Ukrainian and a former officer, former colonel in the Ukrainian army, it was not our role as such, it was not our primary mission. But I take your point, and it's quite significant information and worthy of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my second question, which to some extent you've answered, is: You have no recollection, at any time whilst you were in the enclave, of the Ukrainians complaining about the matters contained within this report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I can recall no such -- I'm struggling here to my memory, but we were billeted with them down there. Obviously, I would have deferred all of this to Viktor because he's the Ukrainian in the former military, but I can recall neither Viktor or them conveying this to us, to the absolute best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your recollection, when you were billeted with the Ukrainian troops, is that they did have fire-arms, presumably.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they -- they had -- I think they had their weapons, as I recall. I can't remember that specifically, but they were not -- it's hard for me to recall their state of military equipment, but -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll just play you a little bit of the video that we have just seen, which was the very first point in which we saw OP2 and its entrance. It's at approximately -- excuse me. It's at approximately 11.35 of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may be that I'm looking at a different video. I'm going to leave this, I'm going to leave this. It is not of sufficient importance. I'm going to move on to another subject and perhaps come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the negotiations that were being carried out locally and which you were, to some extent, party to. You have explained that those negotiations were primarily conducted by the civilian representatives of the Bosniak population, and indeed we can see that in the video clip we saw earlier. We saw Mr. Torlak there and a man who I think is called -- a man you couldn't recognise. I think he's called Mr. Kudovac [phoen], a local doctor. And you've explained that you found it slightly problematical that these local civilian leaders were involved in the negotiations and not the military leaders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Colonel Palic was involved in discussions with the Serbs, and so it was not exclusively that there were only civilians who were in contact with the Serb military. Colonel Palic also had his conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The issue was this question of surrender and whether these individuals were competent to effect a surrender. That's what was the -- that one aspect of it that came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to discuss matters in a private setting with Mr. Torlak as to what he was trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably had an opportunity, but I'm not sure that we had that conversation, to be honest with you. We were -- by the time I saw Torlak and had that dinner where I think he was, that wasn't the issue. We were all simply focused on getting these women out safely. That was our primary preoccupation. After that, I don't recall many separate conversations, if any, with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I am going to accept that that was Torlak's initial concern, to get the civilian population evacuated, but thereafter he engaged in a deliberate tactic of trying to stall the Serbs so as to enable the military men to make good an escape, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On what basis am I supposed to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, he may have told you. You may have gathered that from the negotiation.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you here, speaking under oath, I don't recall any conversation with a man that I can remember about his tactics, his motives. That, I honestly, genuinely don't recall that thing. Whatever -- whatever he had in his mind and whatever his motives were for whatever he said, I'm at pains here -- at quite some difficulty to convey that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one other related subject. You, as you've told us, went to Zepa basically for a day on the 20th of July. You then left and went back to Sarajevo. You then returned on about the 26th of July. In those six days, were you party to any discussions with high-level Bosniak leadership in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I had a meeting with Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And documents would indicate, I think I can put it like this, that Muratovic was heavily involved in this particular sequence of events. Did you discuss with Muratovic what you had seen in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you, the -- I don't really recall what the discussion is. I know I saw it on some of the documents about the proofing. But I think the general aspect of the conversation was more about the prisoner exchange position. But whether I said something about what I'd seen at OP2, I hadn't gotten into Zepa. I don't know if I conveyed something to him or not about what I'd seen at OP2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you discuss with him this concern about the local Bosniak leadership trying to negotiate a deal which, apart from anything else, they probably couldn't deliver on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, and I don't recall and don't believe that I would have raised that. I don't know that I was even aware of that at that time. It didn't come up, and it didn't really impress me as an issue until that meeting where General Smith was there, and then I became more involved and aware of what the essence of these conversations were. I don't believe that I discussed that with Muratovic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you about is your knowledge and awareness of the fighting that was going on in and around Zepa. I want to suggest to you that at various times there was a fierce battle going on between Serb troops, on the one hand, and Colonel Palic's troops, on the other. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the extent of the fighting, but the fact that there would be engagements is -- I think we understood that there might well have been engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You became aware that the men had fled to the hills?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on the 20th of July, you've described hearing some military activity or seeing some military activity on the part of the Serbs. Do you have any idea, at that point in time, where Colonel Palic's brigade was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, and nor do I know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you returned on the 26th and 27th, a similar question?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, yes, we saw Colonel Palic there. We saw him in the town. His unit, his soldiers, we did not see, except for the wounded, the ones both seriously and lightly. No, I had no meetings and never went up for any meeting with them in the hills or to see their condition, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a subject I'll return to in a few moments with the aid of some documents. But before I do that, you were asked by Mr. Thayer about Colonel Palic and your assessment of him and how he handled the situation. You were there when he was seized. Did you at that time feel guilty about witnessing those events and allowing him to be seized?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't know, I wouldn't use the word "guilty," but I think we felt a sense of responsibility that here, look, this is UNPROFOR compound, this is -- the UN is participating in this evacuation, here's a guy who is an interlocutor in these events and then he's being seized, and so, yes, I think I would say I felt a sense of responsibility, and I would add I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And is that personal responsibility or responsibility on behalf of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how does that responsibility manifest itself, if at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you say you feel a sense of responsibility. Have you done anything about it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- since that time, I have tried to engage officials in the international community to make themselves aware that there is inherent UN responsibility in this, that this guy was seized from a UN compound, in a UN-declared safe area during a UN-effected or cooperated operation, and I have met with Palic's wife, Esma, and I have worked to get her meetings with senior officials in the international community, including the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have described to the Trial Chamber your conversations with a number of the Bosniak women prior to their evacuation, and your attempts to find out if they -- to gauge whether they actually wanted to depart or not. To what extent had you sought permission from the Serbs to have those conversations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I need permission from the Serbs to have such a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's not -- the question is: To what extent did you seek a permission? I'm expressing no view as to whether you should or shouldn't have done so. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is negative, and I would infer no objection on the part of the Serbs to -- to such a thing whatsoever. We were -- our role, we were liaising with them, we were talking to them, from Mladic on down, about how we were going to effect all this. I don't recall why I would need to consult with them on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A small related point. The video clip that we saw of the women as they get into the buses, there are a number of men intermingled with the women. That's older men, is it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative, negative. What I would recall, that those would have been the lightly-wounded -- it's possible -- I can't exclude the possibility that there might have been an older -- well over military-aged men in there, but that's less likely. What's more likely is in that footage you have, these lightly wounded, who were themselves desperate to get out and wanted out with this -- with this bus which they presumed to be safe and a safer destiny than to stay with their comrades in the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Josse. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to correct a mistake in the transcript. When you asked me how much time I would need for my cross-examination, I said, "An hour," not that I would not be cross-examining at all. So just to repeat, I will need an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I followed you in French, so I never bothered to check the transcript. So I did distinctly hear that you had cut down your request to one hour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My estimate was mistranscribed as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said 75 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, let me just ask you about your conversation with Mr. Muratovic. Did he make it clear that he was running the Zepa negotiation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear he had a significant role in -- in how -- in terms of determining their position, the Muslim position, absolutely. But whether that was confined to the prisoner issue only, I'm not sure, but it was clear to me he had, yeah, quite a significant position in determining what their position would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were you aware of his line of contact with even Mr. Torlak or with Mr. Palic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to show you a video clip, if we may, please. This, we think, is on the 27th of July. The clip I'm about to show you has some -- have you got anything on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop it there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a Red Cross vehicle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you could tell me the date you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We think this is the 27th of July. We base that on the fact that this is part of a news clip. Give me one moment. I understand that -- do you read this Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, "isti dan".

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that what that is saying is that on the same day at about "5.00 p.m."?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is part of a news clip, and the news reader has above her the date the 27th of July. That's why we're assuming it's that day, but I can't promise you that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you help us about that vehicle? Perhaps you'd like it in a bit more context, the clip.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can show me more of the clip, that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, please stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've also got the advantage of, presumably, understanding what's being said there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't hear, sort of muffled, but he's talking about the evacuation of the wounded. If I understood, he said "ucerk" [phoen], so it would have been the day prior, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what was the Red Cross vehicle doing there, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were there as part of that evacuation of the wounded. However, that was at OP2, and we might have been down at -- in the town, so perhaps they had come back to OP2 and we were not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Explain that, sir. I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary that ICRC would report to us all of their movements. My clear recollection was that their role in this evacuation was confined to the evacuation of the wounded, and they were present when this selection was made with a Serb military doctor and an UNPROFOR doctor. And I understood it -- my recollection is that there was ICRC present during that. Remember, most of our time was spent in that center of town. OP2, where that appears to be, and there's an ICRC vehicle. Maybe they came back, maybe they were present. I can't exclude the possibility that they may have been present. My recollection was that their role was confined to that wounded evacuation, but they might have been around because possibly they were anticipating that there might be a movement of the military men, which of course they would be very likely engaged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay, yes, that's enough on that clip. Thank you very much. What I'd like to ask you now is: on the 20th of July, what time did you leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's very hard to ask for precision about dates, let alone times, so far after the fact. My -- we would have arrived late in the afternoon, because we had gone through all these check-points, Rogatica, et cetera, so we would have arrived late -- in the -- already in the afternoon sometime, and we would have spent this time with General Mladic and -- et cetera. So it would have been rather late in the day, but it was certainly not nightfall when we left on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, again, can you help us, in July, when it gets -- when nightfall -- dusk, what time is dusk in Bosnia in July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be -- it's hard for me to say, but I don't know if it's 8.00 or later. It could be even later. I think it might well even be 8.30 or so at night, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D133, please. This is a similar UNPROFOR document to the one we looked at before. It's dated the 20th of July. The time might be important on some of these. If we look at the bottom left-hand corner of the box there, it says: "ACC CLK:1930". Can you help with that abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say again, sir, where do you want me to help?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bottom left of the box. The large box, that we see, it's got handwritten: "Time, 1930".

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know what that means, but it might well be a received time. I don't know. This was -- this was their military -- we didn't use this same abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then we see: "Alpha" --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's 1900B July '95, so that refers --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the message being sent at 1900 hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the standard date time: 20, 1900 hours, bravo July '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "DMZ Zepa," can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presumed -- what was meant to have been, demilitarised zone, Zepa, presumed, I guess location where this thing, this message was generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the message is, "the fighting between BSA and ABIH with using SA and mortars begun."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "SA" being small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be the military action that you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- it could well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go straight to 6D91, please. This appears to be 50 minutes later. We go down, I'll read this slowly. I've been told I was reading a bit too fast before. I apologise: "Three mortar rounds directly targeted the barrack of UKRCOY. Numerous explosions registered in the UKRCOY enclose. Also UKRCOY camp has been hit with SA and HMG, origin of fire is ABiH." So, again, it appears that the fighting is really getting going at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you want me to help you with any of the initials, I can. "COY" is "Company" and "HMG" is "heavy machine-gun."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have any recollection of having any discussion, either that day or six days later, with the Ukrainians about the fact that their enclosure was coming under attack from Bosniak soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that is, no, I do not recall any such conversation, and nor do I recall any communication from Viktor Bezruchenko, who was Ukrainian and former military, about that. That's my best recollection. I simply don't recall any communication with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's see how it develops. 6D92, this appears to be at 2026 the same day, and again I'll read it: "ABiH is firing at UKRCOY camp with HMGs. Bosnian soldiers had thrown several grenades into the UKRCOY enclose. Ukrainian personnel took its defensive positions, but didn't respond yet. Situation is extremely critical." And, again, you've no recollection of the fact that this happened filtering back to you either that day or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, help us, failure on the part of the United Nations? Or it wasn't important to you, or time lapse, memory gone? Help us as to what you think the reason you can't remember this is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an entirely fair question, and all I can tell you is I don't recall, and I don't -- I just simply don't recall this, this aspect of it. And I should add it doesn't mean we didn't have some conversation about this. It's 2007. These events were in 1995. There's certain events that stand out vividly and there are others that are muddled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting Colonel Palic on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I recall not meeting him on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's of some relevance to the next document, which is 6D87. This is 2000 hours, same day. "The commander of Bosnian 'BD'" - presumably "brigade" - "in Zepa, Avdo Palic, announced that if the helicopter with representatives of BHC FWD --" could the document be made more legible? Thank you very much. "UKRBAT-1, UNHCR, UNMOs doesn't arrive to Zepa by 210800B95, Bosnians will kill Ukrainians." First of all, the abbreviations, "BHC forward"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina Command Forward, that's the UNPROFOR headquarters at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next question: Were you at any stage aware that Colonel Palic had made a threat of this sort?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware because -- of this threat because it had been in discussions, and we had raised this with -- I don't know whether it was myself, but it had been raised, and as I saw in these memoranda that had been written, these reports, it had been raised with Silajdzic, who then denied it, said it wasn't so. But, yeah, I was generally aware that there was this threat. At some point, this was made aware to me. Whether the actual -- I don't recall actually the sit-reps of the specificity of what the Ukrainians were reporting at that time. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell me if this is unfair. In your evidence-in-chief, you gave the impression that you took the view that this allegation about Palic's behaviour was a counter-allegation made by the Serbs in order to try and hide allegations being made against them. What this illustrates is that this allegation was actually coming from the Ukrainian Battalion, themselves. Quite different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I -- I wasn't trying to characterise one way or another the allegations, simply to say that we were aware of it and that the fact was we were told from the Bosnian side that they denied this having happened. What the truth was, I don't know, and I don't know necessarily that these documents are the final word on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Help us as to why these documents are not the final word.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that -- necessarily that they -- that these reports convey with 100 per cent accuracy what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But so we're all clear, there is no question these reports are coming from UNPROFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: These reports are not coming from Serb propagandists, are they?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And nor Serb military, correct, that notwithstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I, of course, accept, because it's written on this piece of paper, it doesn't prove, peradventure, that it's true. Is that what you're saying or are you saying more than that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying even at the time, the absolute accuracy of the origin of the fire and of these reports, I don't know. That's what I'm saying. That's all I can say. I don't know that it is 100 per cent dispositive. If that was actually the event, I think one would have to delve into it further, and I'm certainly not in a position to, with my own awareness, to say it happened that way or it didn't happen that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you went back to organise the evacuation, did it matter at all the way the Ukrainians -- the UNPROFOR troops had been treated by either of the warring parties? Did it matter to your job, in your role?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As remarkable as it may seem to you, sir, it was not our primary preoccupation, nor was it made so by anything that I can recall, myself, in encounters with Ukrainian soldiers with whom we were billeted. I just don't recall that. One might well expect, after being engaged, I think one of their reports said, by heavy machine-gun fire, if you've ever been under heavy machine-gun fire, it gets your attention and you don't forget about it, I simply do not recall that aspect being part of our discussion, nor do I -- obviously, again I would have depended on Viktor to be the primary source for me to pull this from them, but I just don't recall that that was a mission focus of ours, and nor did the Ukrainian soldiers there make it one of ours, as far as I can recall. I cannot exclude the possibility that there was some conversation about this, but it's simply -- it's not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other question on this document. And, by all means, have a look at it again. What do you understand this document is purportedly saying that Avdo Palic wants?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's purporting to say -- it's rather clear. He's making a mortal threat against these UNPROFOR troops. That's what it's conveying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But what does he want? What is it that he's asking to happen in order for him not to go around murdering Ukrainian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's -- according to this document, it's conveying that he wants this arrival of these representatives by a certain time, by the 21st, as it says on its face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were you aware that there was an issue as to whether these representatives were going to go, they were being called for, that sort of thing, because it might help us verify the truth of the document if we can establish that you're aware that Palic wanted this to happen. Of course, it goes some way to proving the truth of the contents.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My short answer to you is, no, I'm not aware of this. At the time, though, it appears the document was generated on the 20th, we had already been there. The representatives that he's seeking, most of us had been there. We -- you had had a representative of UNHCR, you had had an ICRC representative, and you had had us as UNPROFOR forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fairness, though, as you've already explained to us, a number of these organisations were very, very reluctant to get involved, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, you'd have to speak to them as to their reluctance. The fact of the matter is at that initial meeting, you had an UNHCR representative and you had an ICRC representative there at that initial encounter on the 20th. That is my best and clear recollection is they were there the first time, but UNHCR did not come back the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you've told us Palic, himself, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on. 6D135, please. This is a different type of document. It's an UNPROFOR document, but it's a report from Mr. Harland to Mr. Ryan. It's dated the 23rd of July, and I would like, if we may, to turn to the second page, middle paragraph, because it deals with your meeting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the date of the document is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "Civil Affairs sent a team to Zepa on Thursday (20 July) meeting with Generals Mladic and Tolimir, and speaking to the Bosnian commander, Avdo Palic." So stopping there, that is incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you I do not recall meeting Palic on the 20th. That's what I can tell you today, August 2007. I do not recall meeting Palic on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on: "The team confirmed that Zepa was still in Bosnian hands and still intent on resisting, at least until terms acceptable to Sarajevo were offered." Who told you that the Bosniaks were still intent on resisting if you didn't speak to Mr. Palic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that we inferred that from what the Serbs had told us. It's possible that was also our own assessment. It's possible that we inferred that from what the Serbs had told us in conversation with Mladic about the situation, and it's possible, quite possible, that he conveyed his own frustration with their refusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on: "They also learned that two civilian officials from Zepa (the mayor and a young doctor)" - and stopping there, that's obviously Mr. Torlak and also Mr. Kunavac [phoen] - "had met with General Mladic some time the day before, discussing arrangements for surrender and evacuation, but they were unable to confirm whether or not they had accepted Mladic's surrender terms. General Tolimir told the Civil Affairs team that the Serbs would accept an arrangement under which the Muslim population in Zepa could remain, provided that they disarm." Have you mentioned anything about that last paragraph to us before, Mr. Joseph? That last sentence, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't asked about it, and, frankly, you know, I'm not -- I don't recall everything about this until I'm told. And I will tell you, though, as you surely would have seen from other documents, that myself and David Harland had ourselves proposed a demilitarisation agreement for Zepa, had ourselves, on our own initiative, in the interim period, and that I had discussed this with General Tolimir myself, so yes, and I'm quite happy to give you as much as I can recall about why we were pushing for demilitarisation, why I would raise it with General Tolimir and anyone else. I can't specifically tell you why -- I didn't mention this because it didn't pop into my mind, and, frankly, I don't even really remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Isn't it because your evidence actually is far more impressionistic than being an accurate recollection of these events from 12 years ago?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- again, you're asking a witness to characterise his own testimony. I can only tell you -- I cannot going to characterise my own testimony. I'm going to tell you, sir, that I'm conveying to you -- responding to your questions and those of the Prosecution, those of the Court, as best I can, as I can 12 years after the fact. But I'm telling you, if you would like to pursue the questioning about conversation with General Tolimir specifically on the issue of demilitarisation, I'm happy to give you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I accept that you advanced a proposal in that regard, and I've seen that in documentation that has been made available to me. So I'm not going to pursue it, and if it helps, I accept what you've said about that. Just let's look down, please, at the same document. You've got it there: "On Friday, the 21st of July, the Bosnians in the pocket threatened to kill the Ukrainian soldiers in the main base if UNPROFOR did not arrange a meeting between the local commander and the Serbs." So we've got this assertion again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Presumably, your answer is the same as before; no recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not my -- that wouldn't be accurate. I had told you that -- I had told you specifically that I was aware. David and I were both aware of the fact that this threat had been made. We -- and you will see that reported in one of David's reports, wherein he conveys as well that Silajdzic denies it, et cetera. And I'm not putting any judgement on the truth of Silajdzic's reply, either, but I'm telling you it's not true that I wasn't aware. We were aware of some of these threats, and these documents are making it clear, and so there was some awareness on our part of the possible existence of these threats and the fact that perhaps there was even these engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was my fault. I apologise. Thank you for making that clear. Let's have a look, if we may, at 6D134. This is an UNPROFOR report dated the 23rd of July. If we could scroll down, please. It's 0800 hours to 0840 hours, and it says at 800 hours: "Firefight erupted between BSA and BiH in the area of OP1. Both sides engaged SA-MG mortars. ABiH fired with mortars from a firing point located 500 metres close to the UKRCOY base at BSA positions in the direction of OP1." So clearly fighting going on at that time. The reason I've shown you this document is whether you discussed with Muratovic the ongoing fighting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't recall. It's possible that we did, but I honestly don't recall. And from the memoranda that I've seen, it seems like the main subject of the meeting was prisoner exchange and dynamics, a question about what would be possible, politically, in terms of the disposition of the enclave. But I don't recall that. It doesn't mean that we did not discuss that. We might well have left that for the UNPROFOR military to take that issue up with the armija military, which would have been the normal thing, but -- that would have been the normal procedure, for those types of things to be done military to military, but it's possible that it might have come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to move on to 6D29, which is a document that the Trial Chamber have seen before. It's a memorandum from Mr. Ryan to -- to Mr. Ryan from Mr. Harland, dated the 26th of July, as I've said: "Situation in Zepa." Could we scroll down, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says: "At 11.30 p.m. last night, Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter gave the following assessment of the situation in Zepa, as it stood when he left several hours previously." At "ii": "Bosnians, other than men of military age, were coming down from their hamlets in their hills into the Serb-controlled villages and were waiting to be moved by Serb buses to the confrontation line near Kladanj. Many houses in the hills were burning, apparently torched by departing Bosnians." Were you aware that civilians had been sent to the hills?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, but it's -- if the town was being shelled, it would be logical that they would have sought shelter in the hills. But specific awareness of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any torching policy by the departing Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and nor did I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "iii," it goes on: "The Bosnian men of military age were still in the hills, and were apparently awaiting assurances that they would be able to escape to join their families." And that is a position I think we can agree, that they were still in the hills.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, in fairness, this appears to be -- relate to a report of the 25th of July, even though it's dated the 26th, because it's the day before, and you weren't there on that particular day, as you've told us; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it refers to which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's dated the 26th of July, but it refers to the day before, when you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I think the best thing would be to speak to Colonel Baxter. I can note his deliberate use of the word "apparently" in "apparently torched," and suggesting that he, himself, wasn't sure about that, and nor am I. I would just emphasise, nor am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you have a look now at 6D136, please. This is a slightly different type of document, so you may have to help us with what it is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. This is the UNMO, those are the military observers, and it's from their UNMO Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we move it to the second page, please. I'm not sure I've said it's dated the 30th of July. The bottom of the page, it says: "Update from Zepa. Four UNMOs remain in the Zepa pocket and have maintained regular contact with UNMO HQ at Sarajevo." Stopping there, on the 30th of July, were you still in the pocket?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that date. We'd have to use some other means, some other document that establishes my whereabouts. I can't be sure of the date. It's possible I was still there on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to leave the next sentence. Moving on one: "The team are currently located at OP2 and have been restricted to this location since arrival in the pocket. Team stated that the French delegation entered Zepa town today and have confirmed that UNMO equipment ..." Can we turn the page, please: " ... Is still with the UKRCOY. Attempts will be made to extract this equipment 31st July. Team reported hearing intensive shelling on 29th July (23 explosions, 8 HMG bursts and 4 to 6 outgoing mortar rounds) but could not confirm firing points and impact areas. Team did not hear any firing activity today." The reason I'm showing this to you is it confirms, doesn't it, on the 29th of July there was still quite intense fighting going on between the Serb forces and the Bosniak counterparts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that -- yeah, they're hearing intensive shelling, but they're counting that, yeah. I don't know, 23 explosions, 8 heavy machine-gun bursts and 4 to 6 mortar rounds, I don't know how much that qualifies. I mean, Sarajevo would receive thousands of shells, so I'm not sure what this -- you know, how to qualify it in terms of its intensity. But, yes, it would appear, definitely, that there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where this leads me is: Your awareness of fighting, when you had returned there on the 26th of July and thereafter. You must have been aware that these two armies were still engaged in a battle.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, we -- I recall as soon as the last bus had left, that the Serbs had -- Serb army had overtaken our position and was fanning out, and then we had the subsequent meeting with Colonel Kusic. I may well have heard some of this engagement. There may well have been some firing that we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, you don't dispute that there was military activity after the civilians had been evacuated --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- on the 28th, 29th, 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was. I saw the evidence of the -- of this movement, and presumably there quite well could have been. What was the nature of the engagement, from which side did these things originate, or was it even an exchange, that part I can't tell you, but, sure, the possibility that there was fighting, absolutely, very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say I've about 15 or so minutes to go. There's one particular unrelated document I want to show the witness. I certainly don't want to start with that today. I'd ask the Court to rise now, if that's not inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll just do that, Mr. Josse, and we will continue tomorrow. I'm sorry, Mr. Joseph. My anticipation was wrong. We still have a few more cross-examinations to go, but I'm pretty sure we'll finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of August, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
